extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal practitioners, policy officials, and general readers interested in U.S. administrative law
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of the U.S. Administrative Procedure Act (APA), summarizing its purposes, definitions, procedural distinctions (rulemaking vs adjudication), standards of judicial review, publication requirements, and related institutional practices. Useful as a reference for understanding how federal agencies promulgate rules and how courts review agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies must keep the public informed
rubrics_metrics.description: to require agencies to keep the public informed of their organization, procedures and rules
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as one of the basic purposes of the APA (from the Attorney General's Manual): agencies have a duty of public disclosure about how they are organized and operate. No detailed implementation guidance on this page, but the principle underlies publication requirements (Federal Register) and public notice procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public participation in rulemaking (notice and comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: to provide for public participation in the rulemaking process, for instance through public commenting
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The APA's basic purposes include ensuring public participation. The article references Notice of Proposed Rulemaking as the mechanism for proposed rules and ties public commenting to the rulemaking process; see also links to 'A Guide to the Rulemaking Process' and Federal Register guidance. (Implicitly supports the notice-and-comment obligation for substantive rulemaking.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform standards for formal rulemaking and adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: to establish uniform standards for the conduct of formal rulemaking and adjudication
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The APA was intended to create well-defined, uniform procedures for agencies' rulemaking and adjudication. The page contrasts formal (trial-like) and informal procedures and explains that formal procedures create a record subject to judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the scope of judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: to define the scope of judicial review
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One basic purpose of the APA is to set out standards and limits for courts' review of agency action; the article explains statutory and case-law limits (e.g., judicial standards like 'arbitrary and capricious' and 'substantial evidence', and that Congress may limit review by authorizing statutes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'agency' (5 U.S.C. 551(1)) and its exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA in 5 U.S.C. 551(1) defines an 'agency' as 'each authority of the Government of the United States, whether or not it is within or subject to review by another agency', with the exception of several enumerated authorities, including Congress, federal courts, and governments of territories or possessions of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes courts have held the U.S. President is not an agency under the APA; the statutory definition and its exclusions determine which institutions and officials are subject to APA procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal adjudication requirements (trial-like procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal adjudication involve a trial-like hearing with witness testimony, a written record, and a final decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Report (and APA framework) distinguishes formal from informal adjudication: formal adjudication produces a record of proceedings and a final decision and therefore may be subject to fuller judicial review (e.g., substantial evidence review). Informal adjudication instead uses inspections, conferences and negotiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for non-formal rulemaking: 'arbitrary and capricious'
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA requires that to set aside agency actions that are not subject to formal trial-like procedures (i.e. rulemaking), the court must conclude that the regulation is 'arbitrary and capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with the law'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arbitrary and capricious review is more deferential to agencies than substantial evidence review; it allows agency decisions to stand as long as an agency can give a reasonable explanation for its decision based on the information it had at the time. The article references case law and statutory text (5 U.S.C. §706(2)(A)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for formal rulemaking/adjudication: 'substantial evidence' on the whole record
rubrics_metrics.description: To set aside formal rulemaking or formal adjudication (trial-like procedures), agency decisions must be supported by 'substantial evidence' after the court reads the 'whole record'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial evidence review allows courts to consider whether an agency's factual and policy determinations were warranted in light of all the information before the agency at the time, and is thus less deferential than arbitrary-and-capricious review. The article explains that 'whole record' review can involve lengthy records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congress may limit judicial review by statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may further limit the scope of judicial review of agency actions by including such language in the authorizing statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that statutory language can narrow judicial review even when the APA establishes general review standards; agencies and courts interpret authorizing statutes when determining reviewability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 702 waiver of sovereign immunity (right of review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 702 of the APA waives sovereign immunity, allowing people to sue a federal agency in court for non-monetary relief, such as an injunction or a declaratory judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory waiver is the jurisdictional basis for many APA lawsuits seeking relief against agencies; the page cites 5 U.S.C. §702 and notes some limits (e.g., certain monetary claims must be brought in the Court of Federal Claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and promulgation requirements (Federal Register and CFR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and regulations issued or proposed by federal administrative agencies are published chronologically in the Federal Register. Promulgated rules and regulations are then organized by topic in a separate publication called the Code of Federal Regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication in the Federal Register and codification in the CFR are the formal mechanisms for public notice and accessibility of proposed and final rules; the article links to 'A Guide to the Rulemaking Process' and the Federal Register as resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of OIRA and presidential influence on regulatory review
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the Executive Office of the President is the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), a federal subagency led by a presidential appointee that is widely viewed as working on the president's behalf during the regulatory review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes OIRA as a locus of presidential influence over regulatory proposals and cites scholarship on its role. This is an institutional fact that affects how agencies' rulemaking is reviewed and potentially revised before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Report organization: rulemaking vs adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: The Final Report organized federal administrative action into two parts: adjudication and rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This organizational distinction underlies many APA procedural rules: rulemaking (including notice and comment) and adjudication (formal vs informal) have different process requirements and review standards. The article explains the historical rationale for distinguishing them.
